Failure of fusion of the medial nasal process with the maxillary process.

manas.q: Which ear problem is common in children with cleft palate?

children.note: Same order every time so nothing is missed.
Patient details and date, PA or AP, rotation (clavicle heads equidistant from spinous processes), inspiration, penetration.

manas.q: Which quality checks come before interpreting a chest X-ray?

children.note: About 5–6 anterior ribs (mid-clavicular line) or 9–10 posterior ribs above the right hemidiaphragm; poor inspiration crowds vessels and mimics shadowing.

manas.q: How is adequate inspiration judged on a chest X-ray?

children.note: Airway (trachea), Breathing (lungs, pleura), Cardiac (size, borders), Diaphragm, Everything else (bones, soft tissue, lines).

manas.q: What does the ABCDE approach to a chest X-ray cover?

children.note: Apices, behind the heart, hila, costophrenic angles and below the diaphragm — where TB and masses hide.

manas.q: Name the review areas on a chest X-ray.

children.note: Loss of a normal border localises disease: right heart border = middle lobe, left heart border = lingula, hemidiaphragm = lower lobe.

manas.q: Which lobe is involved when the right heart border is lost?

children.note: First infection; typical of children and also seen in adults with low immunity.
Hilar and right paratracheal nodes are the commonest finding, with or without consolidation.

manas.q: What is the hallmark radiological sign of primary TB?

children.note: Healed primary infection: calcified Ghon focus plus calcified hilar node.

manas.q: What is a Ranke complex?

children.note: Enlarged nodes can narrow a bronchus, causing collapse or ball-valve hyperinflation of a lobe, especially in young children.

manas.q: How can lymph nodes in primary TB affect the airways?

children.note: Reactivation or reinfection in someone with prior immunity.
Cavities, often thick-walled, in apical/posterior upper or superior lower-lobe segments signal infectious disease with high bacillary load.

manas.q: What does cavitation on CXR imply in pulmonary TB?

children.note: Patchy nodules in other lobes from spread along airways; on CT seen as centrilobular nodules and tree-in-bud.

manas.q: How does bronchogenic spread of TB appear on CT?

children.note: Upper-lobe scarring pulls hila upward and the trachea toward the affected side; calcification suggests healing but not cure.

manas.q: What signs show upper-lobe volume loss from old TB?

children.topic: Activity cannot be judged on one film
children.note: Compare with old films and confirm with sputum testing; a single film cannot reliably separate active from old TB.

manas.q: Can a single chest X-ray tell active from old TB?

children.note: Haematogenous spread; may look normal early.
CT shows random small nodules before the plain film becomes abnormal.

manas.q: Which imaging is more sensitive than CXR for early miliary TB?

children.note: Metastases (e.g. thyroid), sarcoidosis, fungal infection (histoplasmosis), pneumoconiosis, healed varicella.

manas.q: Give differentials for a miliary pattern on chest X-ray.

children.note: Commonly a unilateral effusion in younger adults and people with HIV.
Blunted costophrenic angle and a meniscus; an erect PA film usually needs roughly 200–300 mL of fluid to blunt the angle (a lateral film shows less).

manas.q: About how much pleural fluid blunts the costophrenic angle on an erect PA film?

children.note: Detects small effusions, shows septations or loculation and guides safe aspiration.

manas.q: What does ultrasound add in pleural TB?

children.note: Empyema, pleural thickening and calcification, and fibrothorax with a trapped lung.

manas.q: What are late pleural sequelae of TB?

children.note: Well-defined rounded nodule, usually upper lobe, often with calcification and small satellite nodules; must be separated from lung cancer.

manas.q: What is the main differential of a tuberculoma?

children.note: Damage persists after cure and causes lifelong symptoms.
Traction bronchiectasis in scarred upper lobes; causes chronic cough and haemoptysis.

manas.q: Where is post-TB bronchiectasis usually found?

children.note: Fungus ball in an old cavity with a crescent of air above it, moving with position; can cause major haemoptysis.

manas.q: What is the radiological sign of an aspergilloma in an old TB cavity?

children.note: Whole-lung collapse and fibrosis with mediastinal shift toward the affected side and compensatory overinflation of the other lung.

manas.q: Which way does the mediastinum shift in a TB-destroyed lung?

children.note: Chronic structural and functional lung damage after treatment completion: airflow obstruction, restriction, recurrent infection; needs follow-up and rehabilitation.

manas.q: What is post-tuberculosis lung disease?

children.note: Rupture of a cavity can cause pneumothorax or bronchopleural fistula.

manas.q: How can TB cause a pneumothorax?

children.note: Children rarely cavitate; nodes dominate.
Hilar or paratracheal lymphadenopathy is the commonest finding; a lateral view helps when the PA film is doubtful.

manas.q: What is the most common CXR finding in childhood TB?

children.note: A normal CXR does not exclude TB in a child; diagnosis combines contact history, symptoms, testing and imaging.

manas.q: Does a normal chest X-ray exclude TB in a child?

children.note: Lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis: diffuse reticulonodular shadowing with hilar nodes, usually in children over 2 with clubbing and parotid swelling; often mistaken for miliary TB.

manas.q: Which features favour lymphoid interstitial pneumonitis over miliary TB in a child with HIV?

children.note: Low CD4 widens the list; TB is possible at any CD4.
Occurs at any CD4 and becomes more frequent as CD4 falls; lobar or segmental consolidation.

manas.q: At which CD4 levels does bacterial pneumonia occur in HIV?

children.note: Higher CD4: typical upper-lobe cavitary disease. Low CD4: atypical, nodal, effusions or a normal film.

manas.q: How does the TB X-ray pattern change as CD4 falls?

children.note: Usually CD4 below 200; a pneumothorax in an HIV patient should raise PCP; effusions and nodes are unusual.

manas.q: Which CD4 level is typical for PCP and which complication suggests it?

children.note: Advanced HIV: nodules or masses, effusions and mediastinal nodes; tissue is needed to separate from TB.

manas.q: What chest imaging findings suggest HIV-associated lymphoma?

children.note: Advanced HIV: nodules, masses or consolidation with nodes; look for meningitis too.

manas.q: What lung findings can cryptococcus cause in advanced HIV?

children.note: After starting ART, films can worsen: larger nodes, new infiltrates or effusions despite effective TB treatment.

manas.q: What imaging changes suggest TB-IRIS after ART is started?

children.note: Tools beyond the plain film.
Shows tree-in-bud, small cavities, miliary nodules and nodes with low-density centre and rim enhancement typical of TB.

manas.q: Which CT features suggest tuberculous lymphadenitis?

children.note: Ground-glass shadowing can be seen on CT when the CXR is normal.

manas.q: What can CT show in PCP when the chest X-ray is normal?

children.note: Focused Assessment with Sonography for HIV-associated TB: pericardial and pleural effusion, ascites, abdominal nodes, spleen and liver micro-abscesses.

manas.q: What does a FASH ultrasound look for?

children.note: Software that reads CXRs and scores the likelihood of TB.
WHO (2021) allows CAD in place of human readers to interpret digital CXR for TB screening and triage in people aged 15 and over.

manas.q: For whom does WHO allow computer-aided detection for TB screening?

children.note: CAD gives a score; programmes set a local threshold, and anyone above it needs bacteriological testing such as Xpert.

manas.q: What must follow an abnormal CAD score?

children.note: Not diagnostic; performance varies by device, population, HIV and prior TB; not yet recommended under 15 years because evidence is lacking.

manas.q: What are the limits of CAD for TB?

children.note: Patterns that mimic TB.
TB, lung abscess (often dependent segments), squamous carcinoma, Klebsiella or staphylococcal pneumonia, fungi, granulomatosis with polyangiitis.

manas.q: List differentials of a cavitating lung lesion.

children.note: TB, lymphoma, sarcoidosis, metastases.

manas.q: Give differentials for hilar lymphadenopathy.

children.note: PCP, pulmonary oedema, viral pneumonia.

manas.q: Give differentials for bilateral perihilar shadowing.

children.note: High-yield points.

children.topic: Normal CXR ≠ no TB in HIV
children.note: Advanced HIV and young children may have TB with a normal film; test sputum anyway.

manas.q: Does a normal CXR exclude TB in advanced HIV?

children.note: CXR is a screening and supporting tool; confirm with Xpert, smear or culture whenever possible.

manas.q: What confirms pulmonary TB after an abnormal CXR?

children.note: Think PCP or cavitating TB.

manas.q: What should a pneumothorax in an HIV patient make you think of?

children.note: How screening guidance compares.
Supports CXR for systematic screening; for people with HIV, combines a four-symptom screen (cough, fever, weight loss, night sweats) with CRP, CXR or molecular tests.

manas.q: What does the WHO four-symptom TB screen ask about?

children.note: Kenya's TB, leprosy and lung disease guideline places CXR within its screening and diagnostic algorithms; check it for local pathways.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline sets TB screening and imaging pathways?

children.note: Papers read on 2026-10-16.

manas.q: How did CXR compare with symptom screening for TB in the 2022 Cochrane review?

manas.q: What did the 2022 meta-analysis find about AI accuracy for pulmonary TB?

children.note: Narrative review: reported AI-assisted CXR programmes found more cases with better accuracy and turnaround in high-burden LMICs; one pathway can screen several chest conditions.

nodeData.note: Consent, confidentiality, negligence, records, P3 and PRC forms, assault care, deaths, autopsy and court duties. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: The principles and the body that hold Kenyan doctors to account.
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice (Beauchamp and Childress); used to analyse ethical dilemmas.

manas.q: What are the four principles of biomedical ethics?

children.note: Kenya Medical Practitioners and Dentists Council registers and licenses doctors and dentists, sets conduct standards and handles complaints.

manas.q: What are the main functions of the KMPDC?

children.note: A complaint to KMPDC is investigated and may go to an inquiry; outcomes range from no action to sanctions on registration.

manas.q: What happens when a complaint is made to KMPDC?

children.note: Doctors should hold indemnity cover so patients harmed by negligence can be compensated and the doctor is defended.

manas.q: Why should a doctor hold professional indemnity cover?

children.note: Permission given by a capable, informed patient acting freely; without it, treatment can amount to assault.
Capacity, adequate information, voluntariness (no coercion) and understanding, followed by a decision.

manas.q: What are the elements of valid consent?

children.note: Nature and purpose of the procedure, benefits, material risks, alternatives (including no treatment) and who will do it.

manas.q: What information must a patient receive before consenting?

children.note: Implied (e.g. offering an arm for BP), express verbal, and express written; written for surgery, anaesthesia and high-risk steps.

manas.q: What are the types of consent?

children.note: Functional test: can the patient understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a decision? Capacity is decision-specific.

manas.q: How is decision-making capacity assessed?

children.note: A capable adult may refuse treatment even if unwise; document the discussion and the refusal.

manas.q: Can a capable adult refuse life-saving treatment?

children.note: When a patient lacks capacity and delay would cause serious harm, give only necessary treatment in their best interests.

manas.q: How is an unconscious emergency patient treated without consent?

children.note: Usually a parent or guardian consents; a mature minor's views matter. Confirm Kenyan legal ages with your lecturer.

manas.q: Who generally consents for treatment of a child?

children.note: Not a signature: discuss, check understanding, allow questions and time, and record what was said.

manas.q: Why is consent described as a process rather than a form?

children.note: A duty to keep patient information private, owed even after the patient dies.
Trust: patients disclose fully only if they expect privacy; breaches can lead to disciplinary and civil action.

manas.q: Why is medical confidentiality important?

children.note: Patient consent; required by law (e.g. notifiable diseases); court order; serious risk of harm to others; need-to-know within the care team.

manas.q: When may a doctor disclose confidential information?

children.note: When disclosure is justified, share only what is needed, with the right person, and document the reason.

manas.q: What rule limits a justified disclosure?

children.note: Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 treats health data as sensitive personal data needing extra safeguards.

manas.q: How does Kenya's Data Protection Act 2019 classify health data?

children.note: Civil wrong where a doctor's failure to meet the expected standard harms a patient.
Duty of care, breach of that duty, causation, and damage; the claimant must prove all four.

manas.q: What four elements must be proved in medical negligence?

children.note: Arises once a doctor-patient relationship exists, e.g. when a doctor agrees to assess or treat.

manas.q: When does a duty of care arise?

children.note: Not in breach if acting as a responsible body of medical opinion would; a common-law standard from England (1957).

manas.q: What is the Bolam test?

children.note: The supporting medical opinion must withstand logical analysis; courts can reject illogical opinion (England, 1997).

manas.q: How did Bolitho refine Bolam?

children.note: The breach must have caused the harm, often tested by asking whether harm would have occurred 'but for' the breach.

manas.q: What is the 'but for' test of causation?

children.note: 'The thing speaks for itself': harm that would not occur without negligence, e.g. a swab left in the abdomen.

manas.q: What does res ipsa loquitur mean? Give an example.

children.note: Most negligence is civil (compensation); gross negligence causing death may lead to criminal charges.

manas.q: When can medical negligence become criminal?

children.note: Keep within competence, follow guidelines, communicate clearly, document well, report incidents and learn from them.

manas.q: How can doctors reduce negligence claims?

children.note: The record is the doctor's best evidence of what was done and why.
Contemporaneous, legible, dated, timed and signed with name; objective; includes findings, plan and advice given.

manas.q: What are the features of a good medical record?

children.note: Never erase or rewrite; strike through with a single line, then date, time and initial; late entries labelled as such.

manas.q: How should an error in medical notes be corrected?

children.note: Undocumented care is hard to prove ('not written, not done'); notes may be produced in court as evidence.

manas.q: Why are records central in legal proceedings?

children.note: The facility keeps records securely as custodian; patients may request access; release to others follows confidentiality and data protection rules.

manas.q: Who holds medical records and who may see them?

children.note: Extends the host: how to complete the police medical examination form well.
Police issue the P3 when a complaint of assault or injury is reported; the doctor completes the medical section.

manas.q: Who issues the P3 form and who completes the medical part?

children.note: Emergency care must never wait for a P3 or police report; examine and treat, then document.

manas.q: Should treatment wait for a P3 form?

children.note: History given, general condition, each injury, likely weapon type, approximate age of injuries, treatment and the degree of injury.

manas.q: What does the doctor record on a P3?

children.note: Type, exact site from fixed landmarks, size in cm, shape, edges, colour and direction; note healing features to estimate age.

manas.q: How should each injury be described medicolegally?

children.note: Abrasion, bruise, laceration (blunt force); incised and stab wounds (sharp force); firearm wounds; burns.

manas.q: Which wound types suggest blunt versus sharp force?

children.note: Commonly graded using Penal Code terms such as harm, grievous harm or maim; check current definitions and form wording with your lecturer.

manas.q: What categories are used to grade injury on a P3?

children.note: Mark injuries on diagrams; keep opinion within your expertise; keep copies of notes for court.

manas.q: What should a doctor keep after filling a P3?

children.note: Extends the host: the facility record for survivors of sexual violence.
A trained clinician at the health facility; a survivor can receive care without first reporting to police.

manas.q: Must a survivor report to police before receiving post-rape care?

children.note: Consent, history of assault, general and genital examination, samples taken, treatment given, referrals and chain of custody.

manas.q: What does the PRC form document?

children.note: The PRC records medical care and evidence; a P3 may also be filled if the case is reported to police.

manas.q: How do the PRC and P3 forms relate?

children.note: Survivor-centred care that treats, protects and preserves evidence.
Separate consent for examination, sample collection, photographs and release of findings to police; survivor may decline any.

manas.q: What separate consents are needed in a sexual assault exam?

children.note: Private room, chaperone, explain each step, let the survivor stop at any time, and avoid judgement.

manas.q: What makes a sexual assault exam trauma-informed?

children.note: Examine early; swabs, clothing, blood/urine for toxicology; air-dry, label, seal and record chain of custody.

manas.q: How is forensic evidence collected after sexual assault?

children.note: Start as soon as possible and within 72 hours of exposure; follow Kenya ARV guidelines for regimen and follow-up.

manas.q: Within what time should HIV PEP be started after sexual assault?

children.note: Offer as early as possible; oral EC is most effective soon after, and a copper IUD is an option up to 5 days.

manas.q: What emergency contraception options exist after rape?

children.note: STI prophylaxis, hepatitis B and tetanus cover as indicated, injury care, counselling and follow-up testing.

manas.q: What other care is offered after sexual assault besides PEP and EC?

children.note: National guidance including PEP.
Certifying death correctly and knowing when a forensic autopsy is needed.
Part I: chain from immediate cause down to the underlying cause on the lowest line. Part II: other contributing conditions.

manas.q: How is Part I of the cause-of-death certificate structured?

children.note: Do not write 'cardiac arrest' or 'respiratory failure' alone; state the disease or injury that started the chain.

manas.q: Why is 'cardiac arrest' not acceptable as a cause of death?

children.note: If the death is reportable (violent, unnatural, sudden unexplained, suspicious), inform police rather than issuing a certificate.

manas.q: What should a doctor do instead of certifying a reportable death?

children.note: Done to clarify disease and for audit or teaching; requires consent from next of kin.

manas.q: What consent does a clinical autopsy need?

children.note: Requested by police or court to establish cause and manner of death; next-of-kin consent is generally not required.

manas.q: Who requests a medicolegal autopsy?

children.note: Natural, accident, suicide, homicide, or undetermined; distinct from cause and mechanism.

manas.q: What are the categories of manner of death?

children.note: Identification, history and scene information, external then internal examination, samples (histology, toxicology), written report.

manas.q: What are the main steps of a medicolegal autopsy?

children.note: Extends the host: how a doctor gives evidence.
Fact witness reports what they saw and did; expert witness gives opinion based on expertise.

manas.q: Distinguish a witness of fact from an expert witness.

children.note: A doctor summoned to court must attend; failing to attend without good reason can be contempt of court.

manas.q: What happens if a summoned doctor fails to attend court?

children.note: Oath or affirmation; examination-in-chief; cross-examination; re-examination; questions from the court.

manas.q: What are the stages of giving evidence in court?

children.note: An expert's duty to the court overrides duty to whoever called them; separate fact from opinion and admit limits.

manas.q: To whom does an expert witness owe their primary duty?

children.note: Prepare from notes, speak plainly, avoid jargon, answer only the question, and stay calm under cross-examination.

manas.q: How should a doctor prepare to give evidence?

children.note: Landmark common-law cases from elsewhere often quoted in Kenyan teaching; confirm local application.
UK Supreme Court: doctors must disclose material risks a reasonable patient would want; replaced Bolam for consent disclosure.

manas.q: What did Montgomery (UK, 2015) change about consent?

children.note: Australian High Court required disclosure of material risks, even rare ones the patient would care about.

manas.q: What did Rogers v Whitaker establish?

children.note: US federal appeals court (DC Circuit) set a reasonable-patient standard for informed consent disclosure.

manas.q: Which US case set a reasonable-patient consent standard?

children.note: House of Lords: a child under 16 with sufficient understanding and intelligence may consent to treatment ('Gillick competence').

manas.q: What is Gillick competence?

children.note: Recent reviews on error, negligence and consent communication.
Review links fear of lawsuits to defensive medicine and urges error reporting, e-prescribing, risk management and ethical, evidence-based practice.

manas.q: What did a 2022 review recommend to reduce errors and defensive medicine?

children.note: Patient explains back in own words what was discussed; review found benefit in medicine, and a few preliminary trials suggest it helps surgical consent.

manas.q: What is teach-back and how may it help informed consent?

children.note: High-yield points.
Duty, Dereliction (breach), Direct causation, Damage: a widely taught memory aid.

manas.q: What are the 'four Ds' of negligence?

children.note: Ordering unnecessary tests or avoiding high-risk patients out of fear of litigation; it harms patients and wastes resources.

manas.q: What is defensive medicine?

children.note: Bolam: standard of treatment by peer opinion. Montgomery: consent disclosure judged by what the patient would want.

manas.q: Contrast the Bolam and Montgomery standards.

children.note: The 2016 consensus (Sepsis-3) definitions in use today.
Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.

manas.q: What is the Sepsis-3 definition of sepsis?

children.note: An acute rise of 2 or more SOFA points from baseline marks organ dysfunction; baseline is assumed to be 0 unless prior dysfunction is known.

manas.q: How is organ dysfunction identified in Sepsis-3?

children.note: Respiratory (PaO2/FiO2), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular (MAP or vasopressor need), CNS (GCS) and renal (creatinine or urine output).

manas.q: Which six organ systems does the SOFA score assess?

children.note: Septic shock: vasopressors needed for MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids. Hospital mortality >40%, versus >10% in sepsis (Sepsis-3).

manas.q: How is septic shock defined in Sepsis-3, and what mortality does it carry?

children.note: SIRS criteria were removed from the definition (too sensitive, not specific) and the term 'severe sepsis' was abandoned.

manas.q: Which older terms did Sepsis-3 remove from the sepsis definition?

children.note: qSOFA flags risk of poor outcome outside ICU; it does not define sepsis, and SSC 2021 advises against it as a single screening tool.

manas.q: Why should qSOFA not be used alone to screen for sepsis?

children.note: How infection turns into organ failure.
Microbial PAMPs and tissue DAMPs bind pattern-recognition receptors (e.g. Toll-like receptors), releasing cytokines such as TNF, IL-1 and IL-6.

manas.q: How do pathogens trigger the host inflammatory response in sepsis?

children.note: Nitric oxide causes vasodilation; endothelial and glycocalyx injury lets fluid leak into tissues, lowering effective circulating volume.

manas.q: Why do septic patients become hypotensive and oedematous?

children.note: Poor perfusion and mitochondrial dysfunction impair oxygen use; lactate also rises from adrenergic-driven glycolysis, not only hypoxia.

manas.q: Why does lactate rise in sepsis?

children.note: Find the source: it guides antibiotics and source control.
Chest (pneumonia) is the commonest, then abdomen, urinary tract, skin and soft tissue; also lines/devices and CNS.

manas.q: What is the commonest source of sepsis in adults?

children.note: Always consider malaria, typhoid and HIV-associated infections such as TB; test for malaria where endemic.

manas.q: Which infections should be considered in sepsis in a Kenyan setting?

children.note: Spot it early; time to treatment matters.
Fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, new confusion, mottled or cold skin, slow capillary refill and low urine output.

manas.q: List clinical clues that suggest sepsis.

children.note: Heart rate divided by systolic BP; a value above 1 suggests shock even if BP still looks acceptable.

manas.q: What is the shock index and what value suggests shock?

children.note: Take samples fast, but never delay antibiotics for them.
At least 2 sets of blood cultures before antibiotics, provided this causes no significant delay.

manas.q: When should blood cultures be taken in suspected sepsis?

children.note: Above 2 mmol/L is abnormal; 4 or more marks marked hypoperfusion. Repeat if raised to track response.

manas.q: What lactate values matter in sepsis?

children.note: Urine dipstick and culture, chest X-ray, malaria test, wound swabs, ultrasound or CT, and lumbar puncture when safe.

manas.q: Which tests help find the source of sepsis?

children.note: SSC 2021: do not use it to decide whether to start antibiotics; it may help, with clinical review, in deciding when to stop.

manas.q: What role does procalcitonin have in sepsis according to SSC 2021?

children.note: SSC hour-1 bundle; the clock starts at triage (time zero).
Measure lactate; remeasure if the first value is above 2 mmol/L.

manas.q: When should lactate be remeasured in the hour-1 bundle?

children.note: 30 mL/kg crystalloid is triggered by hypotension or by lactate ≥4 mmol/L.

manas.q: What two findings trigger the 30 mL/kg fluid bolus?

children.note: Shock or likely sepsis: within 1 hour. Possible sepsis without shock: assess rapidly, give within 3 hours if concern persists.

manas.q: How does SSC 2021 time antibiotics in sepsis with and without shock?

children.note: Broad-spectrum per local guideline and antibiogram; add MRSA or resistant Gram-negative cover only if risk is high; review daily to de-escalate.

manas.q: How should empirical antibiotics be chosen and reviewed in sepsis?

children.note: Give enough, then stop; overload also harms.
Ringer's lactate or Hartmann's are suggested over 0.9% saline for resuscitation.

manas.q: Which fluid type is preferred for sepsis resuscitation?

children.note: Do not use hydroxyethyl starch; albumin may be added when large crystalloid volumes have been needed.

manas.q: Which colloid must be avoided in sepsis?

children.note: Resuscitation, optimisation, stabilisation and evacuation (removing excess fluid).

manas.q: What are the four phases of fluid therapy in sepsis?

children.note: Prefer dynamic tests (passive leg raise, stroke volume change) over static CVP; capillary refill time can guide alongside lactate.

manas.q: How should fluid responsiveness be assessed in sepsis?

children.note: Noradrenaline is first line; target MAP ≥65 mmHg.
If MAP stays low on moderate-to-high noradrenaline, SSC 2021 suggests adding vasopressin rather than escalating noradrenaline alone.

manas.q: Which drug is added when noradrenaline alone fails to keep MAP up?

children.note: Added when MAP is still inadequate; also an alternative when noradrenaline or vasopressin is unavailable.

manas.q: When is adrenaline used in septic shock?

children.note: For septic cardiomyopathy with persistent hypoperfusion despite adequate volume and MAP, add dobutamine or switch to adrenaline.

manas.q: What is added for septic cardiac dysfunction with ongoing hypoperfusion?

children.note: Start vasopressors via a good peripheral vein rather than delay for a central line; site an arterial line when feasible.

manas.q: Can vasopressors be started peripherally in septic shock?

children.note: Hydrocortisone in persistent septic shock.
Adults with septic shock still needing vasopressors; SSC 2021 suggests IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day, e.g. 50 mg 6-hourly.

manas.q: Which septic patients should receive hydrocortisone, and at what daily dose?

children.note: Remove the focus as soon as practical.
Drain abscesses or empyema, debride necrotising fasciitis, relieve an obstructed infected kidney or bile duct, repair perforations.

manas.q: Give examples of source control in sepsis.

children.note: ICU-level support of failing organs.
For sepsis-induced ARDS use low tidal volume ventilation (6 mL/kg predicted body weight) and prone positioning for severe cases.

manas.q: What ventilation strategy is used for sepsis-induced ARDS?

children.note: Transfuse red cells at Hb below 7 g/dL in most adults; give VTE prophylaxis unless contraindicated.

manas.q: What is the usual transfusion threshold in sepsis?

children.note: Classify by preload, cardiac output (CO) and systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
Low preload, low CO, high SVR: cold, clammy, flat neck veins. Causes: bleeding, vomiting/diarrhoea, burns.

manas.q: What is the haemodynamic profile of hypovolaemic shock?

children.note: Stop the loss and restore volume: crystalloid, and blood products for haemorrhage; permissive hypotension in trauma until bleeding is controlled.

manas.q: How is haemorrhagic hypovolaemic shock treated?

children.note: In bleeding trauma give tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2).

manas.q: Within what time should tranexamic acid be given in trauma?

children.note: High preload (raised JVP, crackles), low CO, high SVR. Causes: MI, arrhythmia, acute valve lesion, myocarditis.

manas.q: What is the haemodynamic profile of cardiogenic shock?

children.note: Urgent revascularisation (PCI) for MI, treat arrhythmia, cautious fluids, noradrenaline for hypotension, dobutamine for low output; mechanical support in specialist centres.

manas.q: How is cardiogenic shock from MI managed?

children.note: Low SVR with normal or high CO early ('warm' shock): bounding pulse, warm peripheries; may turn 'cold' later.

manas.q: What is the haemodynamic profile of early septic shock?

children.note: IgE-triggered mast cell release causes vasodilation, leak and bronchospasm.

manas.q: What causes the hypotension in anaphylaxis?

children.note: Lie flat with legs raised; repeat IM adrenaline; refractory cases need an adrenaline infusion. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only.

manas.q: What is done when anaphylaxis does not respond to IM adrenaline?

children.note: Cord injury, usually above T6, cuts sympathetic tone: hypotension with bradycardia and warm, dry skin.

manas.q: How does neurogenic shock differ clinically from other shock?

children.note: Exclude bleeding first; give fluids, then a vasopressor such as noradrenaline; atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.

manas.q: How is neurogenic shock treated?

children.note: Distributive shock refractory to fluids and pressors, often with low sodium and high potassium; give IV hydrocortisone 100 mg.

manas.q: What is the immediate treatment of adrenal crisis?

children.note: High preload (distended neck veins), low CO, high SVR from blocked filling or outflow.

manas.q: What is the haemodynamic profile of obstructive shock?

children.note: Immediate needle (or finger) decompression, then chest drain; do not wait for X-ray.

manas.q: How is tension pneumothorax treated?

children.note: Beck's triad: hypotension, raised JVP, muffled heart sounds; treat with pericardiocentesis.

manas.q: What is Beck's triad and how is tamponade treated?

children.note: Hypotension with right heart strain; give systemic thrombolysis unless contraindicated.

manas.q: What is the treatment of massive pulmonary embolism with shock?

children.note: Multi-organ effects and life after sepsis.
ARDS, acute kidney injury, DIC, septic cardiomyopathy, liver dysfunction and encephalopathy, which may progress to MODS.

manas.q: Name acute organ complications of sepsis.

children.note: Survivors often have lasting fatigue, cognitive problems, anxiety or PTSD, and higher readmission risk.

manas.q: What is post-sepsis syndrome?

children.note: High-yield points.
Raised by adrenaline, liver failure, metformin and seizures too; read it with the clinical picture.

manas.q: Name causes of raised lactate other than shock.

children.note: High JVP points to cardiogenic or obstructive shock; low JVP to hypovolaemic or distributive.

manas.q: How does the JVP help classify shock at the bedside?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where other guidance differs.
Follow national clinical guidelines and local antibiograms for empirical antibiotics; test for malaria and consider HIV-related infection.

manas.q: What should guide empirical sepsis antibiotics in Kenya?

children.note: The World Health Assembly made sepsis a global health priority in 2017 (resolution WHA70.7), urging prevention, early diagnosis and treatment.

manas.q: When did the World Health Assembly adopt sepsis as a global priority?

children.note: Adult guideline: balanced crystalloids, noradrenaline first, vasopressin second, hydrocortisone for ongoing pressors, antibiotics within 1 h in shock.

manas.q: Summarise key SSC 2021 adult sepsis recommendations.

children.note: APSA-led 2025 Delphi: clinical signs may replace lactate, peripheral pressors and adrenaline are acceptable, empirical antiparasitics if suspected.

manas.q: How does the 2025 Delphi adapt sepsis care to resource-limited settings?

children.note: FEAST (children) and a Zambian adult trial (JAMA 2017) found that aggressive early fluid boluses raised mortality.

manas.q: Which African trials showed harm from aggressive sepsis fluid boluses?

children.note: Risk-stratifies adults with suspected sepsis using the NEWS2 early warning score.

manas.q: Which score does NICE use to risk-stratify adults with suspected sepsis?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-16.
41 experts agreed 30 statements: use mental state, capillary refill and urine output if no lactate; balanced salts; adrenaline if no noradrenaline; peripheral pressors.

manas.q: What did the 2025 Delphi suggest when lactate is unavailable?

children.topic: Fluids in sepsis: what trials show
children.note: Goal-directed protocols, vasopressor-first and fluid-restriction strategies did not change mortality in RCTs; review advises weighing fluids per phase and avoiding starches.

manas.q: Did goal-directed or restrictive fluid strategies cut sepsis mortality in RCTs?

maps.title: HME 601 · In depth: Skin structure and lesion terms

nodeData.topic: Skin structure and lesion terms in depth
nodeData.note: Layers, cells, appendages and functions of skin, and the terms used to describe any rash. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Three layers: epidermis, dermis and subcutis.
Epidermis (stratified squamous epithelium), dermis (connective tissue) and subcutis or hypodermis (fat).

manas.q: What are the three layers of the skin?

children.note: Thick skin on palms and soles has a stratum lucidum and no hair; thin skin covers the rest of the body and bears hair follicles.

manas.q: How does thick skin differ from thin skin?

children.note: What happens in each layer as keratinocytes mature.
Single row of dividing cells on the basement membrane; also holds melanocytes and Merkel cells.

manas.q: What cells are found in the stratum basale?

children.note: 'Prickle cell' layer: keratinocytes joined by many desmosomes; Langerhans cells sit mainly here.

manas.q: Why is the stratum spinosum called the prickle cell layer?

children.note: Cells contain keratohyalin granules and release lamellar-body lipids that seal the barrier; nuclei begin to break down.

manas.q: What happens in the stratum granulosum?

children.note: Flattened dead corneocytes without nuclei, packed with keratin and set in lipid ('bricks and mortar'); shed continuously.

manas.q: What is the structure of the stratum corneum?

children.note: Cells take roughly a month to travel from the basal layer to shedding; this is much faster in psoriasis.

manas.q: Roughly how long does a keratinocyte take to reach the surface, and what speeds it up?

children.note: Four cell types live in the epidermis.
Neural-crest-derived cells in the basal layer that pass melanin in melanosomes to keratinocytes.

manas.q: What do melanocytes do and where do they lie?

children.note: Darker skin has a similar number of melanocytes; colour differs by melanosome size, number and spread.

manas.q: Does darker skin have more melanocytes?

children.note: Dendritic antigen-presenting cells (Birbeck granules on electron microscopy); key in allergic contact dermatitis.

manas.q: What are Langerhans cells and which reaction do they drive?

children.note: Basal-layer cells linked to sensory nerve endings; they sense light touch.

manas.q: What is the function of Merkel cells?

children.note: Below the epidermis: anchoring, strength and cushioning.
Desmosomes join keratinocytes to each other; hemidesmosomes anchor basal cells to the basement membrane.

manas.q: What is the difference between desmosomes and hemidesmosomes?

children.note: Links epidermis to dermis; a split here gives subepidermal (tense) blisters, as in bullous pemphigoid.

manas.q: What kind of blister forms when the basement membrane zone splits?

children.note: Thin upper layer of loose connective tissue in the dermal papillae, with capillary loops and Meissner corpuscles.

manas.q: What is found in the papillary dermis?

children.note: Thick deeper layer of dense collagen (mainly type I) and elastic fibres giving strength and recoil.

manas.q: What gives the dermis its strength and elasticity?

children.note: Fibroblasts make collagen and ground substance; mast cells release histamine; macrophages clear debris.

manas.q: Name three cell types of the dermis and their roles.

children.note: Fat lobules divided by fibrous septa: insulation, energy store and cushioning; Pacinian corpuscles lie deep.

manas.q: What are the functions of the subcutis?

children.note: Hair, glands and nails grow from the epidermis.
Anagen (growth), catagen (regression), telogen (rest). Shedding after illness or childbirth is telogen effluvium.

manas.q: Name the phases of the hair cycle.

children.note: Holocrine glands opening into hair follicles (pilosebaceous unit); absent on palms and soles; androgen-driven in acne.

manas.q: Where are sebaceous glands absent, and what drives them?

children.note: Found over almost all skin, most dense on palms and soles; cool the body; sympathetic nerves using acetylcholine.

manas.q: Which neurotransmitter drives eccrine sweating?

children.note: In axillae and anogenital skin; open into follicles; active from puberty; odour comes from bacterial breakdown.

manas.q: Where are apocrine glands and when do they become active?

children.note: Hard keratin plate made by the nail matrix; toenails grow slower, so toenail changes take longer to clear.

manas.q: Which part of the nail makes the nail plate?

children.note: Why skin failure is dangerous.
Stops water loss and entry of microbes, chemicals and UV; damaged barrier underlies dry, eczematous skin.

manas.q: What does the skin barrier protect against?

children.note: Sweating and changes in dermal blood flow (dilation or constriction) control heat loss.

manas.q: How does skin regulate temperature?

children.note: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in the epidermis to vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol).

manas.q: How does the skin make vitamin D?

children.note: Widespread skin loss or erythroderma causes fluid and protein loss, hypothermia and infection risk.

manas.q: What are the dangers of acute skin failure?

children.note: Lesions that arise first (beyond macule, papule, vesicle, bulla).
Raised, flat-topped lesion over 1 cm wide, often from merging papules; classic in psoriasis.

manas.q: What is a plaque?

children.note: Solid raised lesion over 1 cm, usually reaching deeper into dermis or subcutis.

manas.q: What is a nodule?

children.note: Itchy, short-lived swelling from dermal oedema; each one usually fades within 24 hours (urticaria).

manas.q: What is a wheal and how long does each one last?

children.note: Visible collection of pus; may be infected or sterile (as in pustular psoriasis).

manas.q: Is a pustule always infected?

children.note: Bleeding into skin that does not blanch: petechiae are pinpoint; purpura larger; ecchymosis is a bruise.

manas.q: What distinguishes petechiae, purpura and ecchymosis?

children.note: Small dilated superficial blood vessels visible in the skin.

manas.q: What is telangiectasia?

children.note: Burrow: thin track made by the scabies mite. Comedone: plugged follicle (blackhead or whitehead) in acne.

manas.q: What do a burrow and a comedone indicate?

children.note: Changes that develop from primary lesions or scratching.
Visible flakes of shed stratum corneum, as in psoriasis or tinea.

manas.q: What is scale?

children.note: Dried serum, blood or pus on the surface; golden 'honey' crusts suggest impetigo.

manas.q: What does a honey-coloured crust suggest?

children.note: Erosion: loss of epidermis only, heals without a scar. Ulcer: loss into dermis or deeper, may scar.

manas.q: What is the difference between an erosion and an ulcer?

children.note: Excoriation: scratch mark, implying itch. Fissure: linear crack, e.g. on dry hands or heels.

manas.q: What are excoriation and fissure?

children.note: Thinning of skin: shiny, wrinkled, see-through, with visible vessels; e.g. after potent topical steroid overuse.

manas.q: What does skin atrophy look like and what can cause it?

children.note: Keloid spreads beyond the original wound; hypertrophic scar stays within it. Keloids are commoner in darker skin.

manas.q: How does a keloid differ from a hypertrophic scar?

children.note: Arrangement often points to the diagnosis.
Ring with a clearer centre, e.g. tinea corporis or granuloma annulare.

manas.q: Give two causes of annular lesions.

children.note: Concentric rings with a dusky centre; typical of erythema multiforme.

manas.q: Which condition gives target lesions?

children.note: Confined to one nerve segment on one side, as in herpes zoster.

manas.q: Which infection gives a dermatomal rash?

children.note: Clustered blisters on a red base; typical of herpes simplex.

manas.q: What does a cluster of vesicles on a red base suggest?

children.note: In a line: Koebner response along a scratch, or contact with a plant or object.

manas.q: Name causes of linear lesions.

children.note: Flexures (elbow and knee creases): atopic eczema beyond infancy. Extensor surfaces (elbows, knees): psoriasis.

manas.q: Which conditions favour flexural vs extensor sites?

children.note: Face, V of neck, backs of hands; shaded areas such as under the chin are spared.

manas.q: How do you recognise a photo-exposed distribution?

children.note: Quick tests that sharpen the diagnosis.
Firm rubbing shears off epidermis; positive in pemphigus vulgaris, SJS/TEN and staphylococcal scalded skin.

manas.q: In which conditions is Nikolsky sign positive?

children.note: Pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is scraped off, from capillaries near the surface.

manas.q: What is the Auspitz sign?

children.note: Press a glass slide on the lesion: redness that fades is vasodilation; colour that stays is purpura.

manas.q: How does diascopy separate erythema from purpura?

children.note: Rubbing a lesion makes it swell and redden from mast cell release; seen in mastocytosis.

manas.q: What is Darier sign?

children.note: A system so nothing is missed.
Good light, full exposure with a chaperone as needed; include scalp, nails, mouth and genitals.

manas.q: Which areas are often missed in a skin examination?

children.note: Feel texture, warmth, tenderness, depth and mobility; check if the lesion blanches.

manas.q: What should you feel for when palpating a lesion?

children.note: Skin scraping with KOH for fungi, swab for culture, Wood's lamp, and punch biopsy for histology.

manas.q: Name simple bedside investigations in dermatology.

children.note: A handheld lit magnifier that shows structures not seen by the naked eye; aids pigmented lesions and more.

manas.q: What is dermoscopy used for?

children.note: Skin of colour is the norm for most Kenyan patients; textbooks often show lighter skin.
Inflammation may look violet, dusky, brown or grey rather than red; use warmth, swelling and tenderness too.

manas.q: How may inflammation look in darker skin?

children.note: Post-inflammatory hyper- or hypopigmentation is common and slow to fade in darker skin; warn patients.

manas.q: What often follows inflammation in darker skin?

children.note: Six types (I to VI) based on tendency to burn or tan; types V and VI are darker skin.

manas.q: What does the Fitzpatrick scale classify?

children.note: High-yield contrasts.
Pemphigus: intraepidermal, flaccid blisters, erosions, mouth involved. Pemphigoid: subepidermal, tense blisters, elderly.

manas.q: Contrast pemphigus vulgaris and bullous pemphigoid.

children.note: Blanching redness is vasodilation; non-blanching spots are bleeding and may signal sepsis or low platelets.

manas.q: Why does a non-blanching rash matter?

children.note: Only damage reaching the dermis scars; epidermal loss heals completely.

manas.q: Why does an erosion heal without a scar?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Survey of 196 dermatologists in 24 African countries: about half used dermoscopy; main barriers were lack of training and dermatoscopes.

manas.q: What limits dermoscopy use by dermatologists in Africa?

children.note: US review: dark skin is under-shown in textbooks and training, which contributes to missed or late diagnoses.

manas.q: Why does poor skin-of-colour teaching matter?

maps.title: HME 602 · In depth: Rational prescribing and the EML

nodeData.topic: Rational prescribing and the EML in depth
nodeData.note: From choosing a drug to stopping it: EML concepts, dosing, special groups, ADRs and interactions. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Key terms behind the course bubble.
Patients get medicines suited to their clinical need, in doses fitting them, for the right length of time, at the lowest cost to them and society.

manas.q: What is the WHO definition of rational use of medicines?

children.note: The WHO conference of experts that framed rational drug use met in Nairobi, Kenya, in 1985.

manas.q: Where and when did the WHO conference on rational drug use meet?

children.note: Medicines that meet a population's priority health needs, chosen on disease burden, evidence of efficacy and safety, and cost-effectiveness.

manas.q: What are essential medicines and how are they selected?

children.note: Too many drugs per patient, antibiotics for viral illness, injections when oral would do, ignoring guidelines, and self-medication.

manas.q: Give examples of irrational medicine use.

children.note: The template for national lists such as Kenya's.
First published in 1977; WHO revises it every two years.

manas.q: When was the first WHO Model List published and how often is it revised?

children.note: Core: minimum medicines for a basic health system. Complementary: need specialist care, tests or training.

manas.q: What is the difference between the core and complementary lists?

children.note: A separate Model List for children (EMLc) has existed since 2007.

manas.q: Since when has WHO published an essential medicines list for children?

children.note: Access (first/second choice, lower resistance risk), Watch (higher resistance risk, limit use) and Reserve (last resort).

manas.q: What do the three AWaRe antibiotic groups mean?

children.note: Using the current Kenya Essential Medicines List (KEML) at the bedside and in supply.
In public facilities, choose listed generics suited to your level of care so the drug is stocked and affordable.

manas.q: Why should public-sector prescribers choose from the KEML?

children.note: Write the international non-proprietary name: cheaper, avoids brand confusion and allows substitution.

manas.q: Why prescribe by generic name?

children.note: Pharmacy and Poisons Board registers medicines and runs pharmacovigilance; KEMSA supplies public facilities.

manas.q: What are the roles of the Pharmacy and Poisons Board and KEMSA?

children.note: The KEML is meant to be used with national clinical guidelines that set first-line treatments.

manas.q: What should the KEML be used together with?

children.note: WHO Guide to Good Prescribing (1994) method.
Be clear what you are treating and what the treatment should achieve before picking a drug.

manas.q: What two things come first when choosing a P-drug?

children.note: List effective groups and compare them on efficacy, safety, suitability and cost.

manas.q: On which four criteria are drug groups compared?

children.note: Choose the drug within the group, then dosage form, dose schedule and duration.

manas.q: After choosing a group, what else must be decided?

children.note: Confirm the P-drug suits this patient: allergies, interactions, pregnancy, kidney and liver function, cost.

manas.q: What must be checked before giving your P-drug to an individual?

children.note: The best P-treatment may be advice or no drug at all.

manas.q: Is a drug always needed in rational treatment?

children.note: Kinetics that drive dose choice.
Reached after about 4–5 half-lives of regular dosing; same rule for wash-out after stopping.

manas.q: How long does a drug take to reach steady state?

children.note: Loading dose = target concentration × volume of distribution; used when steady state would take too long.

manas.q: What determines the loading dose?

children.note: Depends on clearance: maintenance rate = clearance × target concentration.

manas.q: What determines the maintenance dose?

children.note: Small gap between effective and toxic levels: digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, warfarin, aminoglycosides; monitor closely.

manas.q: Name drugs with a narrow therapeutic index.

children.note: Adjust for the patient in front of you.
Reduce or avoid renally cleared drugs (e.g. aminoglycosides, metformin) by eGFR or creatinine clearance; avoid NSAIDs.

manas.q: How should prescribing change in kidney impairment?

children.note: No single test guides dosing; take care with sedatives and opioids that can tip patients into encephalopathy.

manas.q: Which drugs need special care in liver disease?

children.note: Avoid known teratogens such as warfarin, ACE inhibitors, valproate, isotretinoin, methotrexate and tetracyclines.

manas.q: Name drugs to avoid in pregnancy because of fetal harm.

children.note: Dose by weight (or body surface area), use child formulations; avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome).

manas.q: Why is aspirin avoided in children?

children.note: Lower kidney function and higher drug sensitivity: start low, go slow, review often.

manas.q: What is the prescribing principle for older adults?

children.note: Check whether the drug passes into milk and could affect the baby before prescribing.

manas.q: What must be checked before prescribing in breastfeeding?

children.note: Beyond the basic contents.
Record drug allergies and the reaction type before prescribing.

manas.q: What should be recorded before writing any prescription?

children.note: State dose form, route, frequency and duration or total quantity so the dispenser need not guess.

manas.q: What details stop dispensing errors?

children.note: Opioids and some sedatives are controlled under Kenya's Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (Control) Act; extra rules apply.

manas.q: Which Kenyan law controls opioid prescribing?

children.note: Explain effect, how to take it, common side effects, warning signs and when to return.

manas.q: What should a patient be told about a new medicine?

children.note: Recognise, classify and report.
Predictable, dose-related extension of the drug's action and common, e.g. bleeding on warfarin.

manas.q: What is a type A adverse drug reaction?

children.note: Unpredictable, not dose-related, often immune: anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN. Usually requires stopping the drug.

manas.q: What is a type B adverse drug reaction?

children.note: C chronic (long use), D delayed (e.g. teratogenesis), E end-of-use (withdrawal), F failure of therapy.

manas.q: What do ADR types C, D, E and F stand for?

children.note: Suspected adverse reactions and poor-quality medicines are reported to Kenya's Pharmacy and Poisons Board.

manas.q: Where are suspected ADRs reported in Kenya?

children.note: Pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic.
Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital and St John's wort lower levels of other drugs.

manas.q: Name common enzyme-inducing drugs.

children.note: Macrolides (e.g. clarithromycin) and azole antifungals (e.g. fluconazole) raise levels of other drugs.

manas.q: Name common enzyme-inhibiting drugs.

children.note: Rifampicin makes hormonal contraceptives less reliable; advise a method not affected, such as an IUD or injectable.

manas.q: Why does rifampicin matter for contraception?

children.note: Drugs with added effects, e.g. two sedatives, or two QT-prolonging drugs.

manas.q: Give an example of a pharmacodynamic interaction.

children.note: The last WHO step in depth.
Decide in advance what to check (effect, toxicity, levels) and when.

manas.q: What should a monitoring plan include?

children.note: Planned reduction or stopping of drugs where harm now outweighs benefit, agreed with the patient.

manas.q: What is deprescribing?

children.note: Benzodiazepines, steroids, beta-blockers and antidepressants need tapering to avoid withdrawal or rebound.

manas.q: Name drug classes that need tapering when stopped.

children.note: Simple once-daily regimens, clear counselling and checking cost help patients take medicines as intended.

manas.q: How can adherence be improved?

children.note: Rational prescribing applied to antibiotics.
Right drug, dose, route and duration; take cultures when possible; review at 48–72 hours.

manas.q: What are the core steps of antibiotic stewardship?

children.note: Most upper respiratory infections are viral; antibiotics add harm and drive resistance.

manas.q: Why avoid antibiotics for the common cold?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where others differ.
Current KEML with national clinical guidelines; PPB regulates medicines; KEMSA supplies public facilities.

manas.q: Which documents and bodies guide prescribing in Kenya?

children.note: Model List for adults and children, updated every two years, with AWaRe guidance for antibiotics.

manas.q: What WHO tools support rational prescribing?

children.note: The BNF and BNF for Children are the standard prescribing references; NICE gives guidance.

manas.q: What is the standard prescribing reference in the UK?

children.note: Publishes its own National List of Essential Medicines (latest 2022).

manas.q: What is India's essential medicines list called?

children.note: Beers criteria (American Geriatrics Society) and STOPP/START (Europe) flag risky drugs in older people.

manas.q: Name two tools for spotting inappropriate drugs in older adults.

children.note: High-yield points.
A is common, dose-related, predictable; B is rare, not dose-related, unpredictable.

manas.q: Contrast type A and type B ADRs.

children.note: Adding an inducer can make the other drug fail; stopping it can cause toxicity.

manas.q: Why can stopping an enzyme inducer cause toxicity?

children.note: Rational drug use was defined at a WHO meeting in Nairobi in 1985.

manas.q: Which Kenyan city hosted the 1985 rational drug use meeting?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Review of 74 studies: 16 used the WHO 6-step model; effect was mostly judged by satisfaction or tests, rarely by behaviour or patient outcomes.

manas.q: How is rational prescribing teaching usually evaluated?

children.note: 11 of 12 studies found medical students wrote better prescriptions after added teaching; formal teaching and assessment advised.

manas.q: Does extra prescription-writing teaching help medical students?

children.note: Most trials used medication reviews in primary care; just over half beat usual care on at least one main outcome.

manas.q: How did deprescribing trials in older adults perform?
