nodeData.topic: Nonunion and chronic osteomyelitis in depth
nodeData.note: Why fractures fail to heal, how bone infection persists, and how both are investigated and reconstructed. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: Healing is taking longer than expected for that bone and injury, but is still progressing and may unite without new intervention.

manas.q: What is delayed union?

children.note: Healing has stopped and will not complete without intervention. A widely quoted (FDA) cut-off: at least 9 months after injury with no progress for 3 months.

manas.q: How is fracture nonunion defined?

children.note: A long-standing nonunion in which a fibrous or synovium-lined false joint forms between the fragments, allowing painless or painful movement.

manas.q: What is a pseudarthrosis?

children.note: Persistent or relapsing bone infection, typically beyond about 6 weeks; its hallmark is dead (necrotic) bone harbouring bacteria.

manas.q: What is the hallmark of chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Infection of a fracture site, with or without implants. Confirmed by a sinus or wound breakdown reaching bone/implant, pus, same organism in ≥2 deep samples, or organisms on histology.

manas.q: Which findings confirm a fracture-related infection?

children.note: Key terms for failed healing and persistent bone infection.
Healing needs osteogenic cells, an osteoconductive scaffold, osteoinductive growth signals, mechanical stability and an adequate blood supply. Nonunion means one or more is missing.

manas.q: What are the elements of the 'diamond concept' of fracture healing?

children.note: Absolute stability (compression plating) gives direct healing without callus; relative stability (nails, casts, bridging plates) heals by callus.

manas.q: Which fixation gives primary bone healing and which gives callus healing?

children.note: Tissue formed depends on strain at the gap: under about 2% bone forms, 2–10% cartilage, above 10% only granulation tissue — too much movement blocks union.

manas.q: What does Perren's strain theory predict?

children.note: Bacteria stuck to dead bone or implants live in a protective matrix that resists antibiotics and immune cells — why chronic infection needs surgical removal.

manas.q: Why can antibiotics alone rarely cure chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause; Salmonella is a classic cause in sickle cell disease; open fractures add Gram-negatives and mixed flora.

manas.q: Which organisms commonly cause chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: What bone needs to unite, and why infection persists.
Little or no callus but viable bone ends — often from displacement or a gap; needs reduction and contact, sometimes graft.

manas.q: What is an oligotrophic nonunion?

children.note: Nonunion with infection: treat both — remove dead bone and implants as needed, control infection, then stabilise and reconstruct.

manas.q: What are the principles of treating an infected nonunion?

children.note: I medullary, II superficial (cortex surface), III localised full-thickness but stable, IV diffuse and mechanically unstable.

manas.q: What are the four Cierny–Mader anatomic types of osteomyelitis?

children.note: A: healthy host. B: local and/or systemic compromise (e.g. diabetes, smoking, poor skin). C: treatment would harm more than the disease.

manas.q: What are the Cierny–Mader host classes?

children.note: Types of nonunion and staging of osteomyelitis.
Smoking, diabetes, obesity, malnutrition and long-term steroids all impair healing; optimise them before reconstruction.

manas.q: Which patient factors predispose to nonunion?

children.note: Open and high-energy fractures, bone loss, soft-tissue stripping, infection, inadequate stability or a residual gap.

manas.q: Which injury and surgical factors predispose to nonunion?

children.note: Scaphoid waist/proximal pole, distal-third tibia, femoral neck and proximal fifth metatarsal metadiaphysis (Jones) — all have precarious blood supply.

manas.q: Name four fracture sites prone to nonunion.

children.note: Patient, injury and surgical factors.
Ongoing pain at the fracture, pain on loading, abnormal movement or deformity, and broken or loosening implants.

manas.q: How does a nonunion present?

children.note: Discharging sinus, recurrent flares of pain and swelling, bone thickening and tenderness; fever is often absent between flares.

manas.q: How does chronic osteomyelitis present?

children.note: Late presentation, untreated childhood haematogenous infection and poorly managed open fractures drive much of the burden.

manas.q: Why is chronic osteomyelitis common in low-resource settings?

children.note: How these patients present.
Persistent fracture line, rounded sclerotic bone ends, absent or non-bridging callus; in infection, periosteal reaction, lytic areas and dense sequestra.

manas.q: What X-ray signs suggest nonunion?

children.note: Tibial union score: each of 4 cortices on AP and lateral films scores 1–3 (line visible, callus, bridged); total 4–12.

manas.q: How is the RUST score calculated?

children.note: CT confirms bridging and shows sequestra; MRI maps marrow spread, abscesses and sinus tracts.

manas.q: What do CT and MRI add in nonunion and osteomyelitis?

children.note: FBC, ESR and CRP; normal values do not exclude low-grade infection. In unexplained atrophic nonunion check glucose, vitamin D, calcium and thyroid.

manas.q: Do normal ESR and CRP exclude an infected nonunion?

children.note: Take several deep samples with separate instruments at surgery; avoid sinus swabs, which grow colonisers. Withhold antibiotics beforehand if clinically safe.

manas.q: How should samples be taken to diagnose bone infection?

children.note: Imaging, bloods and sampling.
Stop smoking, control diabetes, correct nutrition and vitamin D deficiency before or alongside surgery.

manas.q: What host measures support nonunion surgery?

children.note: For aseptic femoral/tibial shaft nonunion after nailing: ream and insert a larger nail, or add a plate around the nail.

manas.q: How is aseptic shaft nonunion after nailing managed?

children.note: Iliac crest autograft is the gold standard: it is osteogenic, osteoinductive and osteoconductive.

manas.q: Why is autograft the gold standard bone graft?

children.note: Stage 1: debride and fill defect with cement spacer; a membrane forms over weeks. Stage 2: remove spacer, pack the membrane with bone graft.

manas.q: Describe the Masquelet induced-membrane technique.

children.note: Circular frame with corticotomy and gradual distraction (distraction osteogenesis) grows new bone to fill defects and corrects deformity.

manas.q: How does Ilizarov bone transport fill a bone defect?

children.note: Fix the mechanics, fix the biology, fix the host.
Orthopaedic, plastic surgery, microbiology and infectious diseases together: debride, manage dead space, stabilise, cover soft tissue, target antibiotics.

manas.q: What are the five steps of surgical management of bone infection?

children.note: Remove all dead bone until punctate cortical bleeding (the 'paprika sign') shows healthy bone.

manas.q: What is the 'paprika sign'?

children.note: Antibiotic-loaded PMMA beads/spacers (must be removed later) or absorbable carriers such as calcium sulphate; muscle flaps also fill space.

manas.q: What options exist for dead space management?

children.note: Early infection with a stable implant: debridement, antibiotics and implant retention (DAIR). Late infection or loose implant: remove or exchange.

manas.q: When can an infected fracture implant be retained?

children.note: Long courses, culture-directed: often about 6 weeks if implants removed and up to 12 weeks if retained.

manas.q: How long are antibiotics given for fracture-related infection?

children.note: Considered when the limb cannot be salvaged, the host is class C, or the patient prefers a faster return to function.

manas.q: When is amputation considered in chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Surgery first; antibiotics support it.
Pathological fracture, limb shortening or angular deformity (physeal damage in children), joint stiffness and chronic pain.

manas.q: What local complications follow chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: Long-standing suppuration can cause AA amyloidosis, presenting with proteinuria and renal failure.

manas.q: Which systemic complication can follow years of bone suppuration?

children.note: Infection can flare years or decades later, so follow-up is long and 'arrest' is preferred to 'cure'.

manas.q: Why is chronic osteomyelitis described as arrested rather than cured?

children.note: Long-term consequences.
Screen every nonunion for infection before reconstruction — an occult infection will make grafting fail.

manas.q: Why must infection be excluded in every nonunion?

children.note: Appears denser (whiter) than surrounding bone because it is dead and not remodelled.

manas.q: Why does a sequestrum look dense on X-ray?

children.note: Adding stability alone will not heal an atrophic nonunion — it also needs graft or biological stimulation.

manas.q: Why does rigid fixation alone fail in atrophic nonunion?

children.note: High-yield points.
The Kenya MoH Clinical Guidelines for Level 4–6 hospitals are the national reference for hospital care; check them for local antibiotic and referral advice.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline is the national reference for Level 4–6 hospital care?

children.note: WHO global SSI guidance advises against prolonging antibiotic prophylaxis after the operation ends.

manas.q: Does WHO advise continuing prophylactic antibiotics after surgery?

children.note: International expert group that set the confirmatory and suggestive criteria for fracture-related infection used worldwide.

manas.q: Who defined the criteria for fracture-related infection?

children.note: A 2022 review found FRI consensus authors were mostly from high-income countries; core principles still apply, but infrastructure limits standardisation.

manas.q: How applicable are FRI consensus guidelines to low-income settings?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then international consensus.
Papers read 2026-10-19.
Meta-analysis of 30 studies (38,465 patients): infection raised odds about 7-fold; open fracture, smoking, diabetes and obesity also linked. Evidence mostly low quality.

manas.q: Which risk factor most raised nonunion odds after operated shaft fractures?

children.note: Review of 42 studies (1,605 adults): pooled cure 91% for long-bone chronic osteomyelitis with no clear difference between single- and two-stage surgery.

manas.q: Is two-stage surgery better than single-stage for long-bone chronic osteomyelitis?

children.note: No low-income country authors on FRI consensus papers; diagnosis approach and team working are achievable, but local evidence is lacking.

manas.q: Which parts of FRI consensus are achievable in low-resource settings?

nodeData.note: Safety first, medical causes next: agitation, suicide, delirium, alcohol withdrawal and drug reactions. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What counts as an emergency and the first steps.
An acute disturbance of mood, thought or behaviour carrying an immediate risk of harm to self or others, or of serious medical deterioration.

manas.q: What is a psychiatric emergency?

children.note: Never interview a potentially violent patient alone; keep a clear exit for both of you, know the alarm and remove potential weapons.

manas.q: How do you make the interview setting safe?

children.note: Check airway, vital signs and blood glucose early: an 'acute psychiatric' presentation may be hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, infection or intoxication.

manas.q: Which bedside checks come first in any behavioural emergency?

children.note: Calm words before medicines, medicines before restraint.
One calm staff member speaks; respect personal space, listen, acknowledge feelings, set clear limits and offer real choices (e.g. oral medicine, food, quiet room).

manas.q: Name key verbal de-escalation techniques.

children.note: Last resort: least restrictive, shortest time, trained staff, avoid pressure on chest/neck, continuous observation and full documentation.

manas.q: What are the safety rules for physical restraint?

children.note: After rapid tranquillisation check pulse, BP, temperature, respiratory rate, SpO2 and consciousness regularly until the patient is fully alert and active.

manas.q: What must be monitored after rapid tranquillisation?

children.note: Benzodiazepines: respiratory depression (flumazenil reverses). Haloperidol: acute dystonia, QT prolongation and arrhythmia — get an ECG when possible.

manas.q: What are the main risks of IM benzodiazepines and haloperidol?

children.note: Assess, then make safe.
Asking openly about suicidal thoughts does not plant the idea or raise risk; it often brings relief and opens help.

manas.q: Does asking about suicide increase suicide risk?

children.note: Previous attempt (strongest predictor), depression and other mental disorder, substance misuse, chronic illness or pain, recent loss, isolation and access to means.

manas.q: What is the strongest single predictor of suicide?

children.note: Thoughts, plans, intent, preparations, access to means, lethality of any attempt, hopelessness, and protective factors such as family and faith.

manas.q: What elements make up a suicide risk assessment?

children.note: If risk is imminent: do not leave alone, remove means (pesticides, drugs, sharps), supervised setting, involve family, safety plan and arrange follow-up.

manas.q: What immediate steps protect a patient at imminent suicide risk?

children.note: Medical stabilisation comes first — e.g. pesticide (organophosphate) poisoning, a common method in rural low-income settings.

manas.q: Which self-poisoning is common in low-income rural settings?

children.note: Exclude an organic cause before labelling psychosis.
Acute onset, fluctuating course, inattention and altered consciousness, disorientation, often worse at night; hallucinations are often visual.

manas.q: What are the core features of delirium?

children.note: First episode in later life, sudden onset, abnormal vital signs, disorientation, visual or tactile hallucinations, focal neurology or recent head injury.

manas.q: Which features suggest an organic cause of acute psychosis?

children.note: Hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, sepsis, cerebral malaria, meningitis/encephalitis, HIV-related CNS infection, intoxication or withdrawal, electrolyte, liver or renal failure, drugs.

manas.q: List important organic causes to exclude in acute confusion.

children.note: Glucose, FBC, electrolytes, renal and liver tests, calcium, malaria test, HIV test, urinalysis; CT and lumbar puncture when indicated.

manas.q: What basic tests screen for organic causes of acute behaviour change?

children.note: Treat the cause, reorient, keep family near, good lighting and sleep; low-dose antipsychotic only for severe distress or danger. Avoid benzos unless alcohol/benzo withdrawal.

manas.q: How is delirium managed?

children.note: Can cause vivid dreams, insomnia, mood change and occasionally psychosis — check ARV history in people living with HIV.

manas.q: Which antiretroviral is known for neuropsychiatric side effects?

children.note: From tremor to delirium tremens.
Tremor, sweating and anxiety from 6–24 h after the last drink; seizures mostly 12–48 h; delirium tremens usually from 48–72 h.

manas.q: What is the timeline of alcohol withdrawal?

children.note: Confusion, vivid visual or tactile hallucinations, marked autonomic overactivity and fever; potentially fatal medical emergency.

manas.q: What are the features of delirium tremens?

children.note: First-line: long-acting benzodiazepine (chlordiazepoxide or diazepam); lorazepam if liver failure. CIWA-Ar score can guide symptom-triggered dosing.

manas.q: What is first-line treatment of alcohol withdrawal?

children.note: Confusion, eye signs (nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia) and ataxia; full triad often absent. Give parenteral thiamine before glucose.

manas.q: What is the classic triad of Wernicke's encephalopathy?

children.note: Chronic amnestic state after thiamine deficiency: severe new-learning deficit with confabulation.

manas.q: What characterises Korsakoff syndrome?

children.note: Building on NMS, serotonin syndrome and lithium basics.
High-potency or depot antipsychotics, rapid dose increase, dehydration, agitation and restraint.

manas.q: What raises the risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?

children.note: Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury, aspiration, DVT/PE and seizures; check CK, renal function and urine for myoglobin.

manas.q: What are the major complications of NMS?

children.note: Wait at least 2 weeks after recovery, then a lower-potency or second-generation antipsychotic at a low dose, titrated slowly with close monitoring.

manas.q: How should antipsychotics be restarted after NMS?

children.note: Combinations of SSRIs/SNRIs with tramadol, MAOIs, linezolid, triptans or other serotonergic drugs, or overdose.

manas.q: Which drug combinations trigger serotonin syndrome?

children.note: Diagnosis centres on clonus (spontaneous, inducible or ocular) with agitation, sweating, tremor, hyperreflexia or fever after a serotonergic drug.

manas.q: Which sign is central to the Hunter criteria for serotonin syndrome?

children.note: Stop serotonergic drugs, supportive care and benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine (5-HT2A antagonist) in moderate cases; ICU for hyperthermia.

manas.q: How is serotonin syndrome treated?

children.note: Coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhoea, ataxia, slurred speech, confusion, then seizures and coma.

manas.q: What are the features of lithium toxicity?

children.note: Dehydration, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs and thiazide diuretics raise lithium levels.

manas.q: Which drugs and states precipitate lithium toxicity?

children.note: Take 12 h after the last dose. Usual target about 0.4–1.0 mmol/L; toxicity becomes likely above 1.5 mmol/L.

manas.q: When should a lithium level be taken, and what level suggests toxicity?

children.note: Early extrapyramidal emergencies.
Within hours to days of starting antipsychotics (especially haloperidol), commoner in young men: torticollis, oculogyric crisis, tongue protrusion, trismus.

manas.q: What is acute dystonia and who gets it?

children.note: Rare but life-threatening: stridor and airway compromise — treat urgently.

manas.q: Which form of acute dystonia threatens life?

children.note: Parenteral anticholinergic (e.g. procyclidine, benztropine or biperiden) or diphenhydramine; usually resolves within minutes.

manas.q: How is acute dystonia treated?

children.note: Inner restlessness with inability to sit still; often mistaken for worsening agitation and linked to impulsivity and suicidality.

manas.q: Why is akathisia dangerous to miss?

children.note: A treatable motor syndrome.
Stupor, mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, negativism, staring, echolalia and echopraxia; rated with the Bush–Francis scale.

manas.q: What are the features of catatonia?

children.note: Mood disorders (commonest), schizophrenia, autism, and medical causes such as encephalitis (including anti-NMDA receptor) and metabolic disease.

manas.q: What conditions cause catatonia?

children.note: A benzodiazepine trial is both diagnostic and first-line treatment; a clear response supports catatonia.

manas.q: What is the first-line treatment of catatonia?

children.note: Used when benzodiazepines fail and urgently in malignant catatonia.

manas.q: When is ECT used for catatonia?

children.note: Catatonia with fever and autonomic instability — overlaps with NMS; avoid antipsychotics and treat as an emergency.

manas.q: What is malignant catatonia?

children.note: Dehydration, malnutrition, DVT/PE, pressure sores, aspiration pneumonia and contractures.

manas.q: What medical complications occur in catatonia?

children.note: High-yield points.
Clonus and hyperreflexia point to serotonin syndrome; lead-pipe rigidity with slow reflexes points to NMS.

manas.q: Which examination finding separates serotonin syndrome from NMS?

children.note: In malnourished or alcohol-dependent patients give thiamine before or with glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke's.

manas.q: Why give thiamine before glucose in alcohol-dependent patients?

children.note: New visual hallucinations suggest delirium, intoxication or withdrawal until proven otherwise.

manas.q: What do new visual hallucinations suggest?

children.note: Kenya and WHO first, then where other guidance differs.
Kenya's National Clinical Guidelines for Management of Common Mental Disorders are the local reference for acute care pathways.

manas.q: Which Kenyan guideline covers common mental disorders?

children.note: The mhGAP Intervention Guide supports non-specialists to manage self-harm/suicide, psychosis and substance withdrawal, with explicit emergency steps.

manas.q: What does WHO mhGAP provide for non-specialist health workers?

children.note: UK rapid tranquillisation: IM lorazepam alone, or IM haloperidol with IM promethazine, chosen by history and ECG.

manas.q: Which IM options does NICE NG10 give for rapid tranquillisation?

children.note: Advises against using risk tools or scales to predict suicide or to decide who gets treatment; focus on needs and safety planning.

manas.q: What does NICE 2022 say about suicide risk prediction tools?

children.note: British Association for Psychopharmacology consensus guideline on catatonia: benzodiazepines and ECT central; based mainly on small observational studies.

manas.q: On what evidence is the 2023 BAP catatonia guideline mostly based?

children.note: Papers read 2026-10-19.
Traditional suicide prediction has repeatedly failed; authors propose treating all patients as possibly at risk with person-centred formulation and joint safety plans.

manas.q: Why do authors argue against suicide risk prediction?

children.note: Network meta-analysis of 149 trials: several fixed-schedule benzos cut withdrawal seizures, but only fixed-schedule diazepam cut delirium tremens.

manas.q: Which drug alone reduced delirium tremens in a 149-trial network meta-analysis?

children.note: BAP consensus covers benzodiazepines, ECT and malignant catatonia; trials are rare, so advice rests mainly on small observational studies, case series and reports.

manas.q: What evidence underpins catatonia treatment recommendations?

nodeData.note: Pain mechanisms, causes by site, tests, resuscitation and when to operate. Study aid, reviewed by AI; doctor review in progress — confirm with your lecturer and current guidelines.

children.note: What counts as an acute abdomen and what can mimic it.
Sudden-onset abdominal pain (hours to a few days) from a condition that may need urgent surgery or other urgent intervention.

manas.q: What is meant by the 'acute abdomen'?

children.note: DKA, inferior myocardial infarction, lower-lobe pneumonia, sickle cell crisis, acute porphyria and herpes zoster can all present with abdominal pain.

manas.q: Name medical conditions that can mimic a surgical acute abdomen.

children.note: How abdominal pain is generated and why its site changes.
Dull, poorly localised, felt in the midline; comes from stretch or ischaemia of an organ's wall via autonomic afferents.

manas.q: What are the features of visceral abdominal pain?

children.note: Foregut organs hurt in the epigastrium, midgut in the periumbilical area, hindgut in the suprapubic area.

manas.q: Where is visceral pain from foregut, midgut and hindgut organs felt?

children.note: Sharp, well localised and worse on movement or coughing; arises when inflammation reaches the parietal peritoneum.

manas.q: What causes sharp, well-localised abdominal pain worse on movement?

children.note: Early periumbilical visceral pain shifts to the right iliac fossa once the inflamed appendix irritates parietal peritoneum.

manas.q: Why does appendicitis pain move from the umbilicus to the right iliac fossa?

children.note: Colicky pain suggests obstruction of a hollow tube (gut, ureter); constant pain suggests inflammation, ischaemia or peritonitis.

manas.q: What does colicky abdominal pain usually indicate?

children.note: Recognising the common patterns.
Inspiratory arrest on palpating the right upper quadrant suggests acute cholecystitis.

manas.q: What is Murphy's sign and what does it suggest?

children.note: Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to the back, often eased by leaning forward; gallstones and alcohol are the main causes.

manas.q: How does acute pancreatitis pain typically present?

children.note: Sudden severe epigastric pain that rapidly becomes generalised peritonitis; may follow NSAID use.

manas.q: What is the classic presentation of a perforated peptic ulcer?

children.note: Tenderness at McBurney's point; Rovsing's sign (left iliac pressure causes right-sided pain); psoas and obturator signs for retrocaecal/pelvic sites.

manas.q: Which signs support acute appendicitis on examination?

children.note: Colicky pain, vomiting, abdominal distension and absolute constipation (no stool or flatus).

manas.q: What are the four cardinal features of intestinal obstruction?

children.note: Small bowel obstruction: early vomiting, less distension. Large bowel obstruction: early distension and constipation, late vomiting.

manas.q: How does small bowel obstruction differ clinically from large bowel obstruction?

children.note: Adhesions after surgery and obstructed hernias are leading causes; sigmoid volvulus is an important cause of large bowel obstruction in East Africa.

manas.q: What are common causes of intestinal obstruction in Kenyan adults?

children.note: Colicky pain with drawing up of legs, vomiting, a sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant-jelly stool.

manas.q: What are the classic features of intussusception in an infant?

children.note: Older patient with abdominal or back pain, a pulsatile mass and shock; go straight to theatre if unstable.

manas.q: How does a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm present?

children.note: Tests in order, from bedside to imaging.
Urine dipstick (infection, blood in stones), capillary glucose and ketones (DKA), ECG (inferior MI).

manas.q: Which bedside tests should be done in every acute abdomen?

children.note: FBC, urea and electrolytes, LFTs, amylase or lipase, lactate, blood gas, and group and crossmatch if surgery is likely.

manas.q: Which blood tests are routine in an acute abdomen?

children.note: A level over three times the upper limit of normal, with typical pain, supports acute pancreatitis.

manas.q: What amylase or lipase level supports acute pancreatitis?

children.note: Dilated if small bowel >3 cm, colon >6 cm, caecum >9 cm.

manas.q: What is the 3-6-9 rule on abdominal X-ray?

children.topic: Small bowel vs colon on X-ray
children.note: Small bowel: central, valvulae conniventes cross the full width. Colon: peripheral, haustra cross only part of the width.

manas.q: How do you tell dilated small bowel from colon on X-ray?

children.note: A large inverted-U loop arising from the pelvis on abdominal X-ray suggests sigmoid volvulus.

manas.q: What does the coffee-bean sign on abdominal X-ray suggest?

children.note: Ultrasound is first choice for gallstones, cholecystitis and gynaecological causes, and avoids radiation in pregnancy and children.

manas.q: For which suspected causes is ultrasound the first imaging test?

children.note: Contrast CT is the most informative test for many adult causes, e.g. perforation, obstruction level and ischaemia, if the patient is stable.

manas.q: What is the most informative imaging test in a stable adult with an acute abdomen?

children.note: Migration, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, RIF tenderness (2), rebound, fever, leucocytosis (2), left shift. Total 10; ≥7 makes appendicitis likely.

manas.q: What are the components of the Alvarado score for appendicitis?

children.note: Resuscitate first, then decide on theatre.
ABC, IV access and crystalloid, analgesia, nil by mouth, catheter to monitor urine output, antibiotics if peritonitis or sepsis.

manas.q: What are the first steps in managing a sick patient with an acute abdomen?

children.note: Trials show early opioid analgesia does not reduce diagnostic accuracy or worsen management decisions; do not withhold it awaiting surgical review.
